c: A slab of granodiorite about 112 centimeters tall, carrying one message in three scripts.
Soldiers of a French expedition dug it up in 1799, while rebuilding a fort in the Nile Delta.
Its decree, issued at Memphis in 196 BC, appears in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Greek.
Champollion used it in 1822 to crack the hieroglyphs after fourteen centuries of silence.
It is the British Museum’s most visited object, and shorthand for the key to any puzzle.
w: Three scripts, one message: without it, Egypt’s written past stays sealed.

c: Ten kilos of gold, inlaid with lapis lazuli, quartz, and obsidian.
It was fashioned around 1323 BC for a king who died before his twentieth year.
Howard Carter’s crew opened its case in 1922 and saw “wonderful things” by candlelight.
The striped headdress bears a cobra and a vulture — the Two Ladies of Egypt.
The face of the boy king’s tomb, and of a whole lost dynasty.
w: The boy king was a footnote of history; the mask made him immortal.

c: Thirty-odd bronze gears, corroded and split, pulled from a Roman-era shipwreck in 1901.
Nothing else like it is known for the next fourteen centuries.
Its hand-cranked dials tracked the sun, the moon, and the planets through the zodiac.
It computed the Metonic cycle, predicted eclipses, and even marked the Olympiad games.
Often called the world’s first computer — a Greek astronomical machine from around 100 BC.
w: Someone built a planetarium in bronze a thousand years before clockwork existed anywhere else.

c: A shepherd chasing a stray goat threw a stone into a Judean cave and heard pottery break — so one account goes.
Eleven caves near Qumran gave up fragments of some 900 manuscripts between 1946 and 1956.
Most were written on parchment in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek, some two thousand years ago.
They include the oldest known copies of the Hebrew Bible, a millennium older than anything before them.
Today most of them rest in the Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem.
w: Every modern Bible translation leans, at some verse, on a cave near the Dead Sea.

c: Parian marble, about two meters tall, missing both arms — the holes for her bracelets survive.
A farmer unearthed her in 1820 on the Aegean island of Melos.
She was carved around 100 BC, a blend of Classical ideals and Hellenistic drama.
She may have held an apple — melos means apple — or a shield, or a spindle.
The Louvre’s armless goddess, sold to France within months of her discovery.
w: Two arms are missing; the argument about them never ends.

c: Local well-diggers near Xi’an struck a head of hardened clay in 1974.
An estimated 8,000 soldiers stand in the ranks — and no two faces are alike.
They were painted in bright lacquers that flaked within minutes of excavation.
Each carries real bronze weapons, some still sharp after 2,200 years.
They guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China.
w: One emperor, one afterlife army — bureaucracy rendered in clay.

c: Iron plates, tinned bronze, and garnets — smashed into some 500 pieces and buried in a ship.
It was dug from an East Anglian mound in 1939, on the eve of war.
The face-mask has eyebrows ending in gilded boars, and a dragon flies across the crest.
The 27-meter ship beneath the mound rotted away, leaving only its ghost pressed in sand.
The crowning find of Anglo-Saxon England, probably the grave-goods of King Raedwald.
w: An entire ship dissolved to a shadow in the sand; the helmet refused.

c: Not a tapestry at all: seventy meters of embroidered wool on linen.
Its Latin captions run from 1064 to 1066 and stop mid-scene.
A famous comet streaks across one sky, above frightened courtiers.
It ends with the fall of the housecarls on the ridge near Hastings.
The Normans’ own picture-book of the conquest of England.
w: The winners embroidered their version, and it outlasted every chronicle.

c: Ninety-three pieces of walrus ivory and whale tooth, found in a sand dune in 1831.
Most now sit in the British Museum; Edinburgh holds the rest.
The queens rest their cheeks on their hands; the berserkers bite their shields.
They were carved in Norway around 1150, likely for trade to the Norse isles.
The most famous chess set of the Middle Ages — from the Isle of Lewis in the Hebrides.
w: Vikings played the same endgames we do.

c: A painted limestone core under a coat of stucco, about 47 centimeters tall.
One eye was never finished — a teaching piece, or something stranger.
Ludwig Borchardt’s expedition dug her from a sculptor’s studio at Amarna in 1912.
Her name means “the beautiful one has come,” and her blue crown is like no other queen’s.
She has watched over Berlin for a century, while Egypt keeps asking her home.
w: A portrait so perfect it became a diplomatic problem.

c: Two German hikers found a body melting out of a glacier in 1991 — and assumed it was a modern death.
He carried 61 tattoos, an axe of nearly pure copper, and shoes of bearskin and deer hide.
His last meals were ibex and red deer, einkorn bread, and bracken — his final day was busy.
An arrowhead in his left shoulder, and traces of four others’ blood on his blade, told of a violent end.
Europe’s oldest natural human mummy, 5,300 years old, now rests in Bolzano, Italy.
w: Five thousand years later, we know what he ate for breakfast — and who he fought at the end.

c: A poplar panel, 77 by 53 centimeters — smaller than most hardcover books.
It was never delivered: the artist carried it from Florence toward France, adjusting it for years.
The sitter was Lisa Gherardini, wife of a silk merchant.
In 1911 a handyman walked out of the Louvre with it under his smock; Picasso was briefly a suspect.
Leonardo’s portrait with the famous smile — the most visited painting on earth.
w: The most famous smile in the world was a commission portrait.

c: A canvas painted from memory, looking east before sunrise through a barred window.
The village below is invented; the cypress in the foreground is real.
It was painted in June 1889, from a quiet asylum at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence.
Eleven stars and a wavy moon swirl above a landscape the artist never saw so calmly again.
Van Gogh’s swirling night over Provence — an icon of the Museum of Modern Art since 1941.
w: Painted from an asylum window, and brighter than anything in the sky outside it.

c: A bull, a horse, a light bulb shaped like an eye, a weeping mother — all in black, white, and grey.
It was painted in about three weeks of fury in a Paris studio, in May 1937.
A tapestry copy hangs at the United Nations, where world leaders file past it.
It answered a market town bombed on a Monday, by planes of the Condor Legion.
Picasso’s enormous anti-war painting of a Basque town’s destruction, now at the Reina Sofía.
w: Commissioned for a pavilion, it grew too large for any war but the one it showed.

c: Cast twice, because the first one cracked on its first test ring.
It carries a line from Leviticus: “Proclaim liberty throughout all the land.”
The famous crack grew through decades of ringing, until 1846.
It rang — or so the story goes — for the first public reading of the Declaration of Independence.
Philadelphia’s cracked bell, moved indoors from Independence Hall in 1976.
w: A bell too cracked to ring, and impossible to retire.

c: Spruce and muslin, a twelve-horsepower engine, and a landing gear of skids.
It cost about a thousand dollars and had no wheels — it launched from a rail.
Its longest flight on the first day lasted 59 seconds, into a cold December wind.
The pilot lay prone beside the engine; roll control came from warping the wingtips.
The 1903 Kitty Hawk machine — the first powered airplane, now hanging at the Smithsonian.
w: Twelve horsepower and twelve seconds of flight, and the century turned over.

c: A cone of steel and honeycomb: three couches, five windows, and a heat shield.
While two men walked on the Moon, its pilot photographed the landing site and waited alone for 21 hours.
It splashed down in the Pacific southwest of Hawaii on July 24, 1969, and went straight to quarantine.
Its name was picked at nearly the last minute — after the island of the Statue of Liberty.
Columbia, the command module of Apollo 11, now rests in Washington, D.C.
w: One astronaut kept the ship while the whole world looked at the Moon.

c: A black diorite pillar, 2.25 meters tall, carved with about 4,000 lines of cuneiform.
It was carted off to Susa as war booty around 1150 BC, and dug up again in 1901.
Its prologue says the gods called a king “to cause justice to prevail in the world.”
Law 196 is famous, and grim: an eye for an eye.
Hammurabi’s law code of Babylon, from around 1754 BC — in the Louvre.
w: Justice so old it carved the punishments into stone where nobody could soften them.

c: Sixty-four bronze guns, two decks, and a stern covered in painted lions and Greek heroes.
It sailed about 1,300 meters on its maiden voyage — then heeled, flooded, and sank.
The 1628 disaster killed around thirty people; the inquest blamed nobody by name.
It sat in Stockholm harbor for 333 years, until a wreck-hunter raised it in 1961, nearly intact.
Sweden’s top-heavy royal warship, now the centerpiece of its own museum.
w: A ship that sank in front of half of Stockholm, then waited for them to come back.

c: A 45.5-carat blue stone whose legend keeps accumulating deaths it never caused.
It was cut from the “French Blue,” stolen from the Crown Jewels in 1792.
It glows red under ultraviolet light, phosphorescing for minutes after the lamp goes off.
Its owners’ misfortunes — the newspapers said — ran from a beheaded queen to a sunk liner; the records mostly say otherwise.
The deep-blue diamond mailed to the Smithsonian in a plain brown wrapper, in 1958.
w: A rock with better publicists than geologists.

c: A giant block of Carrara marble, abandoned for decades after two sculptors botched it.
It stands 5.17 meters, its head and right hand enlarged on purpose — for the view from below.
The sling is over the shoulder and the stone hides in the left hand: ambush, not duel.
It took its place outside the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence in 1504, a symbol of the republic.
Michelangelo’s shepherd-giant, now in the Accademia gallery.
w: A block two sculptors ruined, and a 26-year-old who saw the shepherd inside.

c: A single sheet of calfskin, close to A4, in abbreviated Latin — sealed, not signed.
It was annulled by the Pope within ten weeks of Runnymede.
A third of its 63 clauses are about forests; only a few lines of it remain in law today.
“No free man shall be taken or imprisoned...” — clause 39, a seed of due process.
King John’s 1215 Great Charter, the grandfather of constitutional law.
w: A peace treaty that failed in ten weeks and outlived every king who signed it.

c: Nearly a thousand of them, most with bodies buried, ring a remote Pacific island.
They stand with their backs to the sea, eyes once inlaid with coral and obsidian.
The heaviest moved weighs over 80 tons, by a method still argued over — walked upright, some say.
They were carved from a single quarry at Rano Raraku between about 1250 and 1500.
The stone heads of Rapa Nui — Easter Island.
w: Faces for the ancestors, carved until the island ran out of trees to move them.

c: A gravel pit in Sussex gave up skull fragments and a jaw in 1912: England’s first “early man.”
The jaw was stained, the teeth filed flat — quiet doubts simmered for four decades.
He solved an awkward problem: why had England no early humans when France and Germany had plenty?
Fluorine dating raised the flag in 1949; by 1953 he was exposed as a patchwork fake.
The most famous scientific forgery of the century: a medieval human skull and an ape’s jaw.
w: England wanted an ancestor, so somebody arranged one.

c: No single author: a Mainz goldsmith in debt squeezed out about 180 copies in the 1450s, and some 49 survive.
Its two volumes hold 42 lines of type to the page, inked by a press rather than a scribe’s hand.
Copies on paper and on vellum were finished by hand, the red headings brushed in after the press was done.
The first major book of the Western printing revolution, it broke the scriptoria’s thousand-year monopoly.
It carries the name of Johannes Gutenberg, whose workshop launched the age of the printed page.
w: Before it, a book took a scribe a season; after it, a press could make hundreds. Reading, and history itself, never moved the same way again.

c: A barrel of baked clay about 23 centimeters long, covered in cramped little wedges.
The wedges are Babylonian cuneiform, composed in the style of that city’s own royal inscriptions.
It celebrates a conquest won without a battle: Babylon fell to a Persian king in October 539 BCE.
The new ruler let deported peoples go home, which is why one biblical book remembers him kindly.
Written for Cyrus the Great, dug from Babylon’s ruins in 1879, it now keeps quiet in the British Museum.
w: Conquest, propaganda, and a kinder empire than most: an imperial press release in clay, from 539 BCE.

c: A gold funeral face about 30 centimeters tall, beaten from a single sheet with chased detail.
In 1876 it came out of a shaft grave at Mycenae, dug by a German businessman with a gift for timing.
The eyes are slit shut, the mouth is calm, and the hair is braided into rows of tiny curls.
The finder reportedly wired his king that he had gazed upon the face of Agamemnon, and the name never came off.
It is centuries older than the Trojan War of Homer, and whispers of tampering have followed it since the day it surfaced.
w: Schliemann’s timing was perfect and his names were not: the mask is royal, Mycenaean, and about 3,500 years old, but Agamemnon it is not.

c: Four gospels in 340 leaves, made by monks around 800 CE, probably begun on Iona and finished at Kells in Ireland.
Whole pages are surrendered to ornament: animals, knots, and tangled letters teem in colors ground from distant ores.
Viking raids scattered the community that began it, and in 1007 a thief stole its greatest volume from the abbey church for its golden cover.
The book came back within months, its cover gone, and it has been a celebrity of Irish Christianity ever since.
It has lived in the library of Trinity College Dublin since the 1660s, where visitors queue past its open pages.
w: Ireland’s monks called it the great relic of Columba. Call it the most extravagantly decorated book that survives, and few will argue.

c: A two-layer Roman glass: cobalt blue beneath a crust of white, cut away like a cameo to leave figures afloat.
It was made about two thousand years ago, and the scene, gods or lovers or both, has never been settled.
By tradition it was found in an ancient marble coffin near Rome and passed through the palaces of cardinals.
In 1845 a visitor hurled a nearby object at it in the British Museum and smashed it to pieces; it was restored from the shards.
Its name comes from a duke of Portland, and it has stood in the British Museum since 1810.
w: Two millennia of survival, undone in seconds by one man on a spree, then reassembled from a basket of shards.

c: A racing board of twenty squares, its wood inlaid with shell, red limestone, and lapis lazuli.
Players threw tetrahedral dice and raced pieces home, landing on rosette squares for an extra throw.
It was buried in the royal cemetery of Ur around 2600 BCE, among the tombs Leonard Woolley opened in the 1920s.
Its rules survived on a Babylonian clay tablet, decoded in the 1980s by the British Museum’s Irving Finkel.
One of the boards lives in London and a sister in Philadelphia, and both are still perfectly playable.
w: The oldest board game we can still play by its own written rules: five thousand years old, and backgammon is its descendant.

c: A guardian with a bull’s body, eagle’s wings, and a crowned man’s face, worked in five legs.
From the front it stands still; from the side it strides. The fifth leg makes both true at once.
Between its legs, cuneiform credits Ashurnasirpal II with the palace gate it held in the ninth century BCE.
Four meters of gypsum, weighing tonnes, it guarded Nimrud for an Assyrian king who called himself king of the world.
The ones that stayed in Iraq were sledgehammered by ISIS in 2015; the others stand guard in London, Paris, and Chicago.
w: An empire’s doorman, three thousand years on the job, now guarding museum halls instead of kings.

c: A disc of fired clay about 15 centimeters across, stamped on both faces with 241 crisp marks.
The 45 different signs run in a spiral from rim to center, pressed with ready-made seals rather than written by hand.
A Cretan palace gave it up in 1908, in a layer that dates it near 1700 BCE.
Because every mark was stamped, some call it the oldest printed text on Earth, and it certainly is the strangest.
Dozens of scholars have claimed to read it in as many languages, and none of the claims has convinced the others.
w: The world’s most famous unreadable sentence: 45 stamps, one spiral, and thirty-seven centuries of silence.

c: In July 2009 a metal detectorist in a Midlands field heard a signal and started digging into gold.
Out came more than four thousand pieces, nearly all war gear: sword fittings, helmet fragments, and biblical scenes in gold and garnet.
There was not a single coin in the hoard, which is one of its genuine mysteries.
It went into the ground around 650 CE, in the age of Mercia’s warrior kings, and nobody ever came back for it.
The find was valued at 3.28 million pounds, split between finder and landowner, and raised by public appeal in a matter of weeks.
w: Four kilograms of warrior gold, hidden in a field for thirteen centuries, and not a word anywhere about why.

c: Eleven centimeters of limestone, carved while the Ice Age held Europe, about 30,000 years ago.
Heavy hips, folded arms, and braid upon braid of hair, all worked with care, and a face left entirely blank.
Traces of red ochre still ride her surface, the meaning of which went unrecorded.
She was dug from a terrace above the Danube in 1908, near the Austrian village of Willendorf.
She keeps house in Vienna’s Natural History Museum, and the stone she is cut from glitters with tiny fossils.
w: Older than farming, older than writing, older than every king in this puzzle: somebody’s hands made her, and she remains.

c: A hollow wooden box from a royal tomb at Ur, faced with mosaic figures in lapis lazuli and shell.
One long side marches a column of war chariots and trussed prisoners; the other throws a banquet with a lyre player at the center.
It was buried around 2600 BCE in what is now southern Iraq, alongside a king attended by retainers who died to serve him.
Leonard Woolley dug it from the tomb in the 1920s, in fragments he later fitted back together.
Its war and peace panels now anchor the Mesopotamian galleries of the British Museum.
w: Woolley guessed it was a standard carried on a pole, which is where the name comes from, but nobody knows what the box held or why it was buried. The grimmer certainty is the tomb itself: dozens of attendants were arranged to keep serving after death.

c: A marble Nike, the winged goddess of victory, alighting on the prow of a stone warship.
Her gown clings in a sea wind, and the ship’s base is carved as a churning wave.
She was set up in a sanctuary on Samothrace around 190 BCE, most likely to salute a Rhodian naval triumph.
A French consul dug her from the sanctuary in 1863 and shipped her home in pieces.
She now lands headless at the top of the Louvre’s Daru staircase, wings half spread, the most dramatic staircase in any museum.
w: Her arms and head were gone long before excavation; a single upraised hand turned up separately and now lives in a museum in Vienna. The prow beneath her was recovered in later digs, which is why the Louvre display keeps rising off the ground.

c: A carving of Mary holding the crucified Christ across her lap, cut from a single block of Carrara marble.
Michelangelo finished it in 1499, still in his twenties, for a French cardinal’s funeral monument.
It is the only work Michelangelo ever signed: he carved his name across the sash after overhearing visitors credit it to another sculptor.
In 1972 a man with a hammer broke off her arm, nose, and eyelid before guards wrestled him away.
It now stands behind bulletproof glass in Saint Peter’s Basilica in Rome, the first masterpiece of the man who would paint the Sistine ceiling.
w: The signature across Mary’s sash was added in a fit of pride and later regretted; it remains the only sculpture he ever signed. The 1972 attack cost her an arm, a nose, and an eyelid, all restored during months of quiet repair.

c: A 105.6-carat diamond, now mounted in the crown made for the Queen Mother in 1937.
Its name is Persian for mountain of light, and its documented past reaches back to medieval India.
It passed from Mughal emperors to a Persian shah to a Sikh maharaja, each transfer paid in blood or treachery.
In 1850 it reached Queen Victoria under the Treaty of Lahore, and she wore it as a brooch.
India, Pakistan, Iran, and Afghanistan have all asked for it back, and the argument has outlasted every wearer.
w: It was probably mined at Golconda in southern India, and legend says it curses any man who wears it, which conveniently spared the queens. In 1852 Victoria had it recut from 186 carats to its present 105.6, trading nearly half its weight for a brighter sparkle.

c: A Tudor warship that sank in the Solent in 1545 while Henry VIII watched from the shore.
She went down in minutes, leading the English line out against a French invasion fleet.
The fine mud of the seabed sealed her hull, and with it the bones, longbows, dice, shoes, and soup cauldrons of her crew.
She was raised in 1982 before a live worldwide television audience, still cradled in the frame that lifted her.
Her remains now rest in a purpose-built museum at Portsmouth, with bow windows framing the surviving third of her hull.
w: Why she sank is still argued: a gust, a sharp turn with the gunports open, or plain overloading all have their advocates. Hundreds of her crew went down with her, and many of their skeletons show the twisted shoulders of professional archers, bent by a lifetime of the longbow.

c: A single-engine Ryan monoplane named for the hometown of the men who staked the flight.
Because the fuel tank sat directly ahead of the cockpit, Charles Lindbergh steered by periscope and side window.
It was built in about two months in San Diego, fitted with extra tanks holding fuel for a night and a day in the air.
In it, Lindbergh crossed the Atlantic alone in May 1927, New York to Paris in thirty-three and a half hours.
After the flight it never raced again; it went to the Smithsonian, where it hangs beside the Wright Flyer.
w: He carried no radio and no parachute, just five sandwiches, two canteens of water, and a wicker chair; weight mattered more than comfort. The plane made one last flight in 1928, from St. Louis to Washington, and has hung in the Smithsonian ever since.

c: Seventeen colossal basalt heads, some weighing forty tons, carved by Mesoamerica’s first great civilization.
Each wears a rounded helmet with a chin strap and earpieces, gear that scholars link to the ancient ballgame.
They were carved around 1200 to 900 BCE in the lowlands of what is now Veracruz and Tabasco.
The basalt came from the Tuxtlas mountains, and some heads were hauled as far as ninety kilometers with no draft animals and no wheel.
The faces are so individual that most archaeologists read them as portraits of rulers, though no writing survives to name one.
w: The Olmec left no readable script, so the heads are the closest thing to a portrait gallery the civilization has. Everything else claimed about its rulers, names included, is inferred from seventeen faces in basalt.

c: Two over-life-size Greek warriors in bronze, spotted through a diver’s mask off Riace in Calabria in 1972.
The sand had kept them nearly pristine for two thousand years, down to their copper lips and silver teeth.
Each was cast hollow by the lost-wax method, in sections so fine that ancient foundries are still studied through them.
One warrior carries eyes of white stone and the other amber, and both still hold their silver-filled teeth.
They now stand in the museum at Reggio Calabria, generally called the finest original Greek bronzes to survive anywhere.
w: Nobody can name the sculptor; the guesses reach from the circle of Phidias on down, and the argument is half a century old. Hauled up from eight meters of sand by a diver on holiday, they are the closest anyone comes to seeing a Greek master’s bronze as it left the foundry.

c: Thousands of plaques, heads, and figures in brass and bronze once covered the walls of a royal palace in West Africa.
Guilds of master casters made them for the obas of Benin City from perhaps the thirteenth century onward.
Most depict court ceremonies, warriors, and the Portuguese traders who arrived in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
A British punitive expedition seized them in 1897, carrying off the palace’s contents as loot.
They are now spread across dozens of museums, and Nigeria has formally asked for them back.
w: Most are brass, not true bronze, cast by the lost-wax method that survives in Benin City to this day. The looting of 1897 made them some of the most argued-over objects in the world’s museums, and the argument has not cooled.

c: The most complete record of any medieval kingdom, compiled in two volumes by royal scribes.
William the Conqueror ordered the great survey in 1086, twenty years after his invasion of England.
It counts land, ploughs, mills, and people, shire by shire, village by village.
A later cleric compared its rulings to the final judgement, and the nickname stuck for good.
London and Winchester are oddly missing, but the rest of the survey survives complete.
w: A chronicler wrote that no single cow, ox, or pig escaped the king’s notice. The book still lives at the National Archives in Kew, nearly a thousand years after the clerks laid down their pens.

c: An illuminated manuscript of the four Gospels, made around the year 700 on a tidal island off Northumberland.
Bishop Eadfrith of Lindisfarne is credited as its scribe and painter, working alone and in layers.
Its ‘carpet pages’ knot together Celtic, Germanic, and Mediterranean patterns in colors ground from distant minerals.
A tenth-century note between its lines translates the Latin into Old English, the earliest surviving Gospel translation into English.
It has belonged to the nation since the 18th century and is kept today in the British Library in London.
w: Written in honor of St. Cuthbert, it survived Viking raids, the Dissolution, and centuries of damp. Its painted pages are among the greatest things Britain has ever made, and its blues may have crossed the sea from Afghanistan.

c: Jeweled Easter eggs made in St. Petersburg by the House of Fabergé for the last Russian emperors.
The first was an 1885 gift from Tsar Alexander III to his wife, a golden shell hiding a hen, a diamond, and a ruby.
Some fifty imperial eggs were made between 1885 and 1916, and about forty-three have been found.
Each concealed a surprise: a miniature palace, a rosebud, a working model of a Trans-Siberian train.
The revolution ended the series, and the eggs scattered to the Kremlin, to collectors, and to a few still unknown hiding places.
w: Peter Carl Fabergé’s workshop charged the tsars fortunes, and today a single egg can outprice a palace. Eight of the imperial eggs have never been located, and the hunt for them never quite cools.

c: A three-masted wooden frigate launched in Boston in 1797 and still afloat today.
Her oak hull was so tough that enemy shot seemed to bounce off, earning the nickname Old Ironsides.
In the War of 1812 she defeated HMS Guerriere and HMS Java, and took dozens of merchant ships as well.
She never lost a battle, and her victories helped establish the young American navy’s reputation.
She remains a commissioned warship of the United States Navy, berthed at the Charlestown Navy Yard.
w: The oldest commissioned warship still afloat in the world: in 1997, two hundred years after her launch, she sailed Boston Harbor under her own sails one more time, and her crew keeps the rig alive.

c: A slab of dark siltstone carved on both faces, about 63 centimeters tall, found at Hierakonpolis.
One face shows a king in the white crown smiting a foe; the other shows him in the red crown reviewing captives.
Two long-necked beasts twine their necks at its center, and rows of tiny figures stand beneath.
The king named in its hieroglyphs, Narmer, is often identified with Menes, the unifier of Egypt.
It is displayed in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, and may be the oldest historical document on Earth.
w: Around 3100 BCE, a carving that works like political advertising: the first pharaoh, the two crowns, and the smiting pose that Egyptian kings would repeat for three thousand years.

c: A block of red sandstone about 51 centimeters long, kept beneath a throne for seven centuries.
Scottish kings were crowned on it at Scone until Edward I of England carried it off in 1296.
It was fitted into a chair at Westminster, and every British monarch since has been crowned above it.
Four Glasgow students stole it back on Christmas Day 1950, and it broke in two in the process.
It went home to Scotland officially in 1996 and now rests in Edinburgh Castle beside the crown jewels.
w: Also called the Stone of Destiny. In 2023 it traveled south once more for the coronation of King Charles III, hauled to London in a purpose-built case, as it has been for every crowning since 1308.

c: A bronze disc 30 centimeters across, inlaid with gold sun, moon, and stars, dug from a hilltop in Saxony.
The cluster of seven small gold dots matches the Pleiades as seen three and a half thousand years ago.
It was illegally excavated in 1999 with two swords, and recovered by police in a 2002 sting operation.
At around 1600 BCE it is generally called the oldest known concrete depiction of the cosmos.
It is displayed in the State Museum of Prehistory in Halle, Germany, and in UNESCO’s Memory of the World register.
w: The looters’ shovel marks are still part of its story, and so is the layered gold that seems to mark the angle between solstice sunsets. Whoever buried it on the Mittelberg carried a portable sky.

c: An enormous gateway of blue glazed brick, raised in Babylon around 575 BCE.
King Nebuchadnezzar II built it as the grand entrance to the city’s processional way.
Rows of golden lions, bulls, and dragons in molded brick honored Ishtar, Adad, and Marduk.
German archaeologists excavated it in the early 1900s and shipped the pieces to Berlin.
Its reconstruction is the centerpiece of the Pergamon Museum.
w: A king’s gateway of blue brick, now the pride of a museum an empire never imagined.

c: Wall panels of amber, backed in gold leaf, assembled in Prussia at the start of the 1700s.
Frederick William I shipped the whole room to Peter the Great as a diplomatic gift in 1716.
It glowed for two centuries in the Catherine Palace at Tsarskoye Selo.
Nazi occupiers crated it up in 1941 and carried it off to Königsberg.
It vanished in the chaos of 1945 and has never been found.
w: An entire room of amber, gifted, stolen, and lost to the last war.

c: Edvard Munch painted the first version in 1893 and revisited the image for two decades.
A figure clutches its skull-like face on a bridge above the Oslofjord at sunset.
The artist wrote that he sensed an infinite scream passing through nature.
One version was stolen from Oslo’s National Gallery in 1994; another from the Munch Museum in 2004.
Both were recovered, and the paintings are back on Norwegian walls.
w: The modern world’s most familiar shudder, painted four times over.

a: The Girl with a Pearl Earring
al: the girl with a pearl earring
vermeer’s girl with a pearl earring
c: Johannes Vermeer painted her around 1665, in oils the size of a large book.
She is not a portrait but a tronie, a study of an imagined face and costume.
No record names the sitter, which has invited centuries of guessing.
The pearl is likely too large to be real; some suspect a drop of glass, others just paint.
She hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague, often called the Mona Lisa of the North.
w: A stranger with a borrowed pearl who became a Dutch icon.

c: Rembrandt finished it in 1642, the same year his wife Saskia died.
Its proper title names a militia company of Amsterdam under Captain Frans Banninck Cocq.
The canvas was trimmed on all sides when it moved to the town hall in 1715.
Dulled varnish made a daylight scene look nocturnal, and so it earned its nickname.
It survived a knife in 1975 and acid in 1990, and now anchors the Rijksmuseum.
w: A militia portrait so dramatic that people forget it is one.

c: Mary Pickersgill and her seamstresses sewed it in Baltimore in the summer of 1813.
It measures about nine by twelve meters, with fifteen stars and fifteen stripes.
It flew over Fort McHenry through the British bombardment of September 1814.
Francis Scott Key watched it still flying at dawn and put the sight into verse.
The Smithsonian has kept it since 1912, now behind glass in a low-oxygen chamber.
w: A garrison flag that survived a night of shells and gave a country its anthem.

c: Peat cutters found him in a Danish bog in 1950, his face so fresh they called the police.
He died in the fourth century BCE, hanged, with the noose still around his neck.
His last meal was a porridge of barley, flax, and wild seeds.
Only his head and one hand are original; the rest was reconstructed from the bog’s evidence.
He rests at the Silkeborg Museum, calm as a sleeping farmer.
w: A face from the Iron Age, preserved by a bog that kept its secrets.

c: Workers unearthed it near Sidon in 1887, in a chamber of royal tombs.
Its reliefs show Alexander the Great at the Battle of Issus and on a lion hunt.
It likely held Abdalonymos, a gardener made king of Sidon by Alexander’s favor.
Its carvings still carry traces of the paint that once made the marble blaze.
It has been the prize of the Istanbul Archaeology Museums for over a century.
w: A stone coffin that puts Alexander himself in the picture.
